S043.name: Restrictive_Intake
S043.description: Persistent restriction of energy intake relative to requirements, leading to significantly low body weight.

subtypes.Eating Very Small Amounts: Eating only one or two bites a day or extremely small portions per meal.
subtypes.Skipping Meals: Intentionally skipping breakfast, lunch, or dinner.
subtypes.Exclusion of Specific Food Groups: Strictly avoiding specific food groups like carbohydrates or fats to prevent nutritional imbalance.
subtypes.Strict Calorie Restriction: Limiting daily caloric intake to an extremely low level.

S044.name: Low_Weight
S044.description: A body weight that is significantly below the minimum level of health for age, sex, developmental trajectory, and physical health.

subtypes.Continuous Weight Loss: A state where weight continues to decrease due to intentional restriction of intake.
subtypes.Insistence on Low Weight: Attempting to lose more weight or refusing to restore weight despite already being underweight.

S045.name: Fear_of_Weight_Gain
S045.description: Intense fear of gaining weight or of becoming fat, even though at a significantly low weight.

subtypes.Fear of Weight Gain: Extreme fear and loathing of gaining weight or becoming fat.
subtypes.Fear of Specific Foods: Fear that eating high-calorie foods will immediately lead to weight gain.
subtypes.Obsession with Weight Gain: Compulsively checking the scale and becoming extremely anxious about even the slightest increase.

S046.name: Body_Image_Weight_Shape_Disturbance
S046.description: Undue influence of body weight or shape on self-evaluation.

subtypes.Distorted Body Image: Perceiving one's body as much fatter than it actually is or perceiving specific parts as excessively large when looking in the mirror.
subtypes.Self-Worth Dependent on Weight: Judging whether one is a good or successful person solely based on weight or body shape.

S084.name: Low_Weight_Severity_Non_Recognition
S084.description: Persistent lack of recognition of the seriousness of the current low body weight.

subtypes.Denial of Medical Risk: Not admitting or dismissing the health risks caused by being underweight.
subtypes.Disregard of Symptoms: Not taking physical symptoms caused by low weight (dizziness, hair loss, amenorrhea) seriously.
subtypes.Dismissal of Concerns: Exaggerating or rejecting the concerns of doctors or family as unnecessary.

symptom.disease_info: Anorexia nervosa is an eating disorder characterized by persistent restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight, intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, and a distorted perception of one’s body weight or shape or undue influence of weight/shape on self‑evaluation. It often begins in adolescence or young adulthood but can emerge or recur later in life, sometimes in the context of major stressors, health events, or transitions that reactivate longstanding perfectionism or body image concerns. The course can be chronic or relapsing, with medical complications involving multiple organ systems and significant psychosocial impairment even when the individual denies the severity. It is distinguished from other eating disorders by the presence of significantly low weight and a primary focus on restriction rather than recurrent binge‑eating and compensatory behaviors as seen in bulimia nervosa or binge‑eating disorder.

patient.stressor: Raisa’s eating problems re‑intensified over the past two years as she pushed for a tenure‑track position, juggling long hours in the CRISPR lab, grant deadlines, and expectations to keep producing visually polished, high‑impact work for exhibitions. She began treating food as another variable to control in an otherwise unpredictable professional landscape, gradually tightening her intake during late‑night lab sessions and studio marathons, telling herself she was just being efficient and "disciplined" like in her experiments. The competitive academic environment, frequent travel to conferences, and implicit pressure to appear endlessly energetic and composed made it easier to normalize how little she was actually eating, even as colleagues commented on how different she looked. The situation became clinically significant when a collaborator quietly suggested she looked unwell before a major grant presentation, and her spouse, worried about her visible weight loss and mounting exhaustion, insisted she see the campus health service, which then referred her for psychiatric evaluation.
patient.chief_complaint: I’ve gotten so strict about what and when I eat that it feels like I’m constantly cutting back and still telling myself it isn’t enough.

patient.stressor: For Osmany, the turning point came after his divorce and a minor back injury forced him to move out of the family home and briefly reduce his hours at the warehouse. The loss of his daily family routines and shared meals left him eating alone, and he gradually started skipping meals, telling himself it would help his back feel lighter and make dancing and soccer easier once he got back into them. As he lost more weight, coworkers and his soccer teammates commented with concern, but he interpreted their reactions as overprotective and took pride in how "lean" and in‑control he felt, even as basic tasks at work became more taxing and he began struggling to keep up with the physical demands of his job. The condition came to clinical attention only after a near‑fainting episode during a warehouse shift led to an urgent care visit, where lab work and his markedly low weight prompted the physician to recommend psychiatric assessment.
patient.chief_complaint: Everyone keeps saying I’m way too thin and sick, but I honestly don’t see what the big deal is about my weight right now.

patient.stressor: Audrey’s longstanding, quieter preoccupation with food and weight sharpened after she took on coordinating medical appointments and finances for her older sister, who was diagnosed with a chronic cardiac condition. The responsibility amplified her sense that she needed to be "ultra‑disciplined" and healthy herself, and she began meticulously tracking and reducing her intake under the guise of optimizing her own longevity, fitting it neatly into her data‑driven worldview. Over several months, as consulting travel and caregiving demands increased, she found it easier to forgo meals during long stretches of work and hospital visits, subtly reshaping her routines so that eating became an afterthought and her self‑evaluation hinged more and more on how controlled she could keep her body. The issue became clinically significant when her primary care physician, alarmed by her ongoing weight loss at an annual exam and hearing her describe her strict personal "health rules," referred her for psychiatric evaluation despite her insistence that she was simply being careful.
patient.chief_complaint: My sense of whether I’m doing well or not has started to revolve almost entirely around what I weigh and how tightly I’m controlling my shape.
